senses.def: completely necessary or extremely important
examples: Water is essential for life.
It's essential that you arrive on time for the exam.

senses.def: basic and central to the nature of something
examples: The essential difference between the two plans is cost.

senses.def: something that is necessary (usually plural)
examples: We only packed the essentials: water, food, and a map.

senses.def: when you consider the basic or most important nature of something
examples: The two phones are essentially the same, except for the color.
Essentially, he's a kind person who makes bad choices.

senses.def: to start an organization, system, or relationship that is meant to last
examples: The university was established in 1891.
The two countries established diplomatic relations last year.

senses.def: to discover or prove that something is true
examples: Investigators are trying to establish the cause of the fire.
Police have established that he was at home that night.

senses.def: to make people accept you or something in a particular role
examples: She quickly established herself as one of the best lawyers in the city.

senses.def: an organization, business, or institution such as a hotel, store, or restaurant
examples: The restaurant is a family-owned establishment that opened in 1952.
Smoking is banned in all public establishments.

senses.def: the act of starting or creating something
examples: The establishment of the national park protected the forest.

senses.def: the people and institutions that have power and influence in a society (the Establishment)
examples: The candidate ran as an outsider against the political establishment.

senses.def: a large area of land in the country, usually with a big house, owned by one person or family
examples: The family's estate includes a vineyard and a lake.

senses.def: all the money and property a person owns, especially what is left when they die
examples: She left her entire estate to an animal charity.
His estate was worth over $5 million.

senses.def: (British) an area of land with many houses or factories of the same type
examples: He grew up on a housing estate outside Manchester.

note: "Real estate" (gayrimenkul) is very common in American English. A British "estate agent" is an American "real estate agent" or "realtor".

senses.def: a guess of the size, value, or cost of something, made without exact figures
examples: By some estimates, the storm caused $2 billion in damage.
At a rough estimate, about 500 people attended.

senses.def: a written statement of how much a job will probably cost
examples: Get at least three estimates before hiring a contractor.

senses.def: to guess the size, cost, or value of something without calculating it exactly
examples: Experts estimate that the bridge will cost $40 million.
The crowd was estimated at 10,000.

note: Pronunciation differs: noun /ˈestɪmət/, verb /ˈestɪmeɪt/.

senses.def: lasting or existing forever, without an end
examples: Many religions promise eternal life after death.
They swore eternal love to each other.

senses.def: seeming to continue forever, often in an annoying way
examples: I'm tired of their eternal arguments about money.

note: "I'll be eternally grateful" is a common way to give strong thanks.

senses.def: a set of moral principles or beliefs that guide how someone behaves
examples: She has a strong work ethic and never misses a deadline.
The company tries to follow an ethic of honesty with its customers.

senses.def: moral rules for a group or profession, or the study of right and wrong (ethics)
examples: The senator was investigated for violating ethics rules.
She teaches medical ethics at the university.

note: Singular "ethic" mostly appears in "work ethic"; otherwise use "ethics" (takes a plural or singular verb).

senses.def: connected with beliefs about what is morally right and wrong
examples: Cloning animals raises serious ethical questions.
Doctors face ethical dilemmas every day.

senses.def: morally correct or acceptable
examples: Is it ethical to test cosmetics on animals?
She only buys from ethical clothing brands.

senses.def: connected with a group of people who share a culture, language, or origin
examples: The city is home to many ethnic groups.
Ethnic minorities are still underrepresented in Congress.

senses.def: typical of a culture different from the main one in a country
examples: The neighborhood is full of ethnic restaurants.

note: "Ethnic food" is becoming less used; many prefer naming the cuisine (Thai, Ethiopian).

senses.def: the unit of money used in many countries of the European Union
examples: The hotel costs 120 euros a night.
The dollar rose against the euro this week.

note: In Turkish it's "avro" or "euro"; in English the plural is "euros".

senses.def: to move people from a dangerous place to a safer one, or to leave a dangerous place
examples: Thousands of residents were evacuated before the hurricane hit.
Staff had to evacuate the building after a gas leak.

senses.def: to judge the quality, value, or importance of something after careful thought
examples: Teachers evaluate students on homework, tests, and participation.
We need to evaluate the risks before we invest.

senses.def: the act of judging how good, useful, or successful something is
examples: Every employee gets a performance evaluation once a year.
The program is still under evaluation.

senses.def: used to emphasize something surprising or unexpected
examples: He didn't even say goodbye.
Even my grandma has an Instagram account now.

senses.def: used with comparatives to make them stronger
examples: The second movie was even better than the first.

senses.def: flat and smooth, or equal and balanced
examples: Spread the paint in an even layer.
The score was even at halftime.

senses.def: able to be divided exactly by two
examples: Two, four, and six are even numbers.

note: Opposite of an even number is an odd number (tek sayı). "Break even" = neither gain nor lose money.

senses.def: the part of the day between late afternoon and bedtime
examples: We usually go for a walk in the evening.
Are you free on Thursday evening?

senses.def: an event or social occasion that happens in the evening
examples: The school is hosting a music evening for parents.

note: Use "in the evening" but "on Monday evening". "Good evening" is a greeting; say "good night" when leaving.

senses.def: something that happens, especially something important or unusual
examples: The book describes the events leading up to the war.
Her death was a tragic event for the whole town.

senses.def: a planned public or social occasion, or one race or competition in a sports program
examples: The charity event raised over $50,000.
She won gold in the 200-meter event.

note: "In the event of" (formal) = if something happens: In the event of fire, use the stairs.

senses.def: happening at the end of a long process or period of time
examples: The team lost in the semifinals to the eventual champions.
The eventual cost of the project was double the estimate.

note: False friend: "eventual" does NOT mean "possible" (olası). It means what finally happens.

senses.def: at the end of a period of time or a series of events, often after delays
examples: After three hours of waiting, we eventually got a table.
You'll eventually get used to the cold winters here.

note: False friend: NOT "possibly" (Turkish "eventüel/olası"). "Eventually" = in the end.

senses.def: at any time, used mainly in questions, negatives, and comparisons
examples: Have you ever been to New York?
This is the best pizza I've ever had.

senses.def: used to mean "always" or "increasingly" in certain phrases
examples: Prices keep rising ever higher.
They lived happily ever after.

note: Use with present perfect for life experience: Have you ever...? "Hardly ever" = almost never.

senses.def: used with a singular noun to mean all members of a group, one by one
examples: Every student must bring a photo ID to the exam.
I walk the dog every morning before work.

senses.def: used to show how often something happens, at regular intervals
examples: The bus comes every ten minutes.
Take one pill every four hours.

note: Takes a singular verb: Every student has a laptop. "Every other day" = gün aşırı.

senses.def: every person; all the people in a group
examples: Everybody at the party was dancing.
Does everybody have a copy of the agenda?

note: Same as "everyone" but slightly more informal. Singular verb: Everybody is here.

senses.def: happening or used every day; ordinary and normal
examples: Smartphones have become part of everyday life.
These are simple recipes made with everyday ingredients.

note: One word = adjective (everyday clothes). Two words = adverb phrase: I go running every day.

senses.def: every person; all people
examples: Everyone in my family loves soccer.
Thanks, everyone, for coming tonight.

note: Singular verb, but "they/their" is normal: Everyone has their own opinion. "Every one" (two words) = each single item.

senses.def: all things, or all the things in a situation
examples: The fire destroyed everything they owned.
Is everything OK? You look upset.

senses.def: the most important thing to someone
examples: My kids are everything to me.

senses.def: in, to, or at every place
examples: I've looked everywhere for my keys.
There were tourists everywhere in the old city.

senses.def: facts, signs, or objects that show that something is true
examples: There is strong evidence that smoking causes cancer.
Police found no evidence of a break-in.

senses.def: information or objects used in a court of law to prove something
examples: The knife was presented as evidence at the trial.

note: Uncountable: NOT "an evidence" or "evidences". Say "a piece of evidence".

senses.def: clear and easily seen or understood
examples: It was evident from her face that she was upset.
His love for the game is evident in every match he plays.

senses.def: morally very bad and enjoying harming others
examples: The movie is about an evil queen who poisons her stepdaughter.
Slavery was an evil system.

senses.def: great moral wrong, or a force that causes bad things to happen
examples: The story is about the battle between good and evil.
Poverty and disease are the great evils of our time.

note: "The lesser of two evils" = ehven-i şer. Very strong word; for small wrongs use "bad" or "mean".

senses.def: to bring a feeling, memory, or image into your mind
examples: The smell of baking bread evokes memories of my childhood.
The photos evoke the hardships of life during the Depression.

senses.def: the slow development of plants and animals over millions of years as they adapt
examples: Darwin's theory of evolution changed biology forever.
Fossils give us clues about human evolution.

senses.def: the gradual development of something into a different or more advanced form
examples: The museum shows the evolution of the car over 100 years.

senses.def: connected with evolution or with slow, steady development and change
examples: Birds are the evolutionary descendants of dinosaurs.
The new phone is an evolutionary step rather than a revolution.

senses.def: to develop gradually, especially from a simple to a more complex form
examples: The company has evolved from a small shop into a global brand.
Language is always evolving.

senses.def: (of plants and animals) to change over many generations through evolution
examples: Whales evolved from land mammals.

senses.def: correct in every detail; completely accurate
examples: Do you know the exact time the train leaves?
I can't remember his exact words.

senses.def: to demand and get something, often by force (formal)
examples: The gang exacted revenge on the man who betrayed them.

note: "To be exact" adds precision: It took two hours, 140 minutes to be exact.

senses.def: used to say that something is correct in every detail
examples: The meeting starts at exactly 9 a.m.
That's exactly what I wanted to say.

senses.def: used as a reply to show strong agreement
examples: "So we need more time?" "Exactly."

note: "Not exactly" is often ironic or polite: He's not exactly friendly (= he's quite unfriendly).

senses.def: to make something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is
examples: He always exaggerates how much money he makes.
The risks have been greatly exaggerated by the media.

note: Spelling trap: double g, single r. Opposite: understate, play down.

senses.def: a formal test of knowledge or skill, especially at school or college
examples: I have a chemistry exam on Monday morning.
She passed all her final exams with high grades.

senses.def: a medical check of part of the body
examples: You should get an eye exam every two years.

note: "Take an exam" = sınava girmek (NOT "give an exam", which is what the teacher does). Americans also say "test" for smaller exams.

senses.def: a careful look at or study of something or someone
examples: A closer examination of the data revealed several errors.
The doctor performed a full physical examination.

senses.def: a formal test of knowledge or skill (formal)
examples: Candidates must pass a written examination to become lawyers.

note: "Exam" is the everyday word for a test; "examination" is formal.

senses.def: to look at or consider something carefully in order to learn about it
examples: The study examines the effects of social media on teenagers.
Experts examined the painting to see if it was a fake.

senses.def: to look at someone's body carefully to check their health
examples: The doctor examined my knee and ordered an X-ray.

senses.def: something that shows what a group of things is like or supports a general idea
examples: Can you give me an example of a renewable energy source?
Many cities, for example Paris and Amsterdam, have banned old cars.

senses.def: a person or behavior that others should copy
examples: Parents should set a good example for their children.

note: "Make an example of someone" = punish someone to warn others.

senses.def: to be greater than a particular number, amount, or limit
examples: The cost of repairs could exceed $10,000.
He was fined for exceeding the speed limit.

senses.def: to be better than what was expected or hoped
examples: The results exceeded all our expectations.

senses.def: the quality of being extremely good
examples: The hospital is known for its excellence in cancer care.
She received an award for excellence in teaching.

senses.def: extremely good
examples: The food at that restaurant is excellent.
She speaks excellent English.

note: Already very strong, so don't use "very": NOT "very excellent".

senses.def: not including; apart from
examples: The store is open every day except Sunday.
Everyone was invited except me.

senses.def: used before a fact that makes a statement not completely true
examples: I'd love to come, except I have to work that night.
The twins look identical except that one has longer hair.

note: Don't confuse with "accept" (kabul etmek), which sounds similar.

senses.def: a person or thing that does not follow a general rule or is not included
examples: All the rooms were small, with the exception of the kitchen.
Most of the songs were great, and this one was no exception.

note: "Take exception to" (formal) = to be offended by something.

senses.def: unusually good
examples: She's an exceptional student who finished college at nineteen.
The wine from that year was of exceptional quality.

senses.def: very unusual and not likely to happen often
examples: Refunds are only given in exceptional circumstances.

senses.def: an amount that is more than necessary, usual, or acceptable
examples: An excess of salt in your diet can raise blood pressure.
He was known for his life of excess.

senses.def: more than is needed or allowed
examples: The airline charged me for excess baggage.
Cut off any excess fat before cooking the meat.

note: "In excess of" (formal) = more than: in excess of $1 million.

senses.def: much more than is reasonable or necessary
examples: The officers were accused of using excessive force.
Excessive drinking can damage your liver.

senses.def: the act of giving something and receiving something in return
examples: He offered to fix their computer in exchange for dinner.
The two countries agreed to a prisoner exchange.

senses.def: a short conversation or argument, or a visit where people from two countries swap places
examples: There was a heated exchange between the two senators.
She spent a year in Japan as an exchange student.

senses.def: to give something and receive something of the same kind in return
examples: We exchanged phone numbers before saying goodbye.
Can I exchange this shirt for a smaller size?

note: "Exchange rate" = döviz kuru. "Exchange glances/words/gifts" = to give to each other.

senses.def: feeling very happy and enthusiastic, especially about something that will happen
examples: The kids are so excited about going to Disneyland.
I'm really excited to start my new job next week.

note: The person feels excited; the thing is exciting. Use "excited about" (NOT "excited for" in formal writing, though it's common in speech).
